newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korea offered New Year's gift -- food aid.
newsitem.headline: North Korea offered New Year's gift -- food aid.

text.p: SEOUL, Dec 31 (Retuer) - North Korea was offered a New Year's gift from the United States after officials in Washington said they were considering providing more food aid that would stave off looming famine.

Meanwhile, South Korean officials on Tuesday said they were working out details of a briefing on peace talks that Pyongyang agreed to attend after offering an apology to South Korea on Sunday over a submarine incursion.
They said they anticipated a briefing on four-party peace talks offered by the United States and South Korea with North Korean and China late in January.
Cargill, the world's largest grain trading company, was awaiting U.S. Treasury Department approval to sell up to two million tonnes of grain into famine-striken North Korea.
U.S. officials said they were considering easing trade sanctions against North Korea to allow barter deals.
The United Nations World Food Programme is expected to make an official appeal shortly and the United States was expected to offer $6 million, the officials said.
The officials said Cargill may be issued a licence to export an initial 500,000 tonnes of food.
North Koreans have been scrabbling for edible roots to stave off hunger as a result of floods that have devastated harvests for two years running.
With winter approaching -- and fuel oil supplies precariously low -- North Korea is desperate for help to fill its empty graneries.

It was not clear what kind of grain Cargill would try to barter, but analysts in Seoul said the proposed shipment of two million tonnes would go far towards helping the most vulnerable North Koreans -- particularly pregnant women and infants -- survive the cold.

Cargill's application "includes a broad authorisation on what constitutes the business and does not specify, rice, corn or other commodity. But it would be food," company spokeswoman Laurie Johnson told Reuters.
North Korea is 2.3 million tonnes short of its minimum grain needs, according to a report by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation.
On Monday, South Korea returned the ashes of 24 Northern infiltrators shot dead after landing on the east coast by the Shark-class submarine.
The South Korean media reported food aid as well as assistance on building two nuclear reactors for North Korea would resume as early as next month.
But the Foreign Ministry on Tuesday said no details had been settled and South Korea was watching for changes in North Korea's attitude.
"We are watching North Korea's attitude change to decide on a time frame," a senior ministry official said.
"But we will be more flexible with North Korea than before the submarine incursion, and cooperation on light-water nuclear reactors should be renewed soon."
South Korea pledged to supply the reactors after North Korea promised to halt its nuclear weapons programme in a 1994 agreement with the United States.
The foreign ministry official said details were still being worked out on the briefing.
"We have not finalised the details for a formula, but South Korea, North Korea, and the United States would be the countries attending the briefing," he said.
The Chosun Ilbo newspaper cautioned against excessive optimism in an editorial.

"All North Korea did was read an apology, and our media is busily decorating the news with hopeful forecasts," it said. "Giving North Korea everything and playing into their hands is like giving up our national sovereignty."
